At the end of our street stood a red telephone box that no one had used in years. Its glass was scratched, its door hung crookedly, and a small forest of weeds had grown up around its feet. In summer, bees visited the weeds. In winter, the box collected rain.

My grandmother called it the wishing phone.

“If you have something you can’t say to a person,” she told me, “you can say it in there.”

I was nine, and I believed her because she was my grandmother and because the telephone box looked like the sort of place that might keep a secret. I went inside one afternoon with a coin I’d found in the pocket of an old coat. It wasn’t enough to make a call, but I put it in the slot anyway.

“I don’t want to move,” I said into the receiver.

My parents had found a house in another town. It had a garden and a bright yellow kitchen and a room for me under the roof. Everyone kept saying how exciting it was. I had already packed my books, but I hadn’t packed the things that mattered: the cracked blue mug I used as a pencil pot, the stone shaped like a sleeping fox, the paper crown from my birthday.

I put down the receiver. The phone swallowed my coin with a click.

That evening, Grandma asked if I’d used the wishing phone.

“Yes,” I said.

“Did it answer?”

“No.”

She smiled. “Some answers take the scenic route.”

The moving van came on a Tuesday. The house emptied one room at a time. By afternoon, even the echoes belonged to someone else. Grandma stood on the pavement in her wool coat, although it was too warm for one, and held my face between her hands.

“People think leaving is the opposite of staying,” she said. “It isn’t. You take things with you. You also leave things behind. That’s how you know you were here.”

I didn’t understand. I hugged her hard enough to crease her collar, then climbed into the car.

The new house was nice. The yellow kitchen was as bright as promised. My room had a slanted ceiling, and when it rained, I could hear the drops tapping above my bed. I put my books on a shelf and arranged my stones on the windowsill. I even liked the garden, once I got used to the fact that its apple tree never produced apples.

But for weeks I felt like a guest in my own life. At school, nobody knew the stories behind my things. The stone was just a stone. The cracked mug was just a mug. When my teacher asked us to draw a map of somewhere important, I drew our old street. I made the telephone box taller than it really was.

That winter, Grandma became ill.

My mother told me over breakfast, carefully, as if the words were hot. I was old enough to understand what illness meant but too young to imagine its ending. We drove back to the old town on a Sunday. The street looked smaller than I remembered. The telephone box was still there, its red paint faded almost pink.

Grandma was in bed by the window. Her hands looked light, like they could be lifted by a breeze. I sat beside her and told her about school, the apple tree, the fox-shaped stone. She listened as if each detail were a letter arriving from a far country.

When I ran out of things to say, she looked at me.

“Have you been back to the phone?”

“No.”

“You should,” she said. “I think it has something for you.”

After the visit, I walked to the telephone box alone. The weeds were gone, cut back to the pavement. Someone had repaired the door. I stepped inside and lifted the receiver.

There was no dial tone. There was only a faint hum, like a refrigerator in another room.

“I think I’m going to miss you,” I said.

The hum continued.

“I’m sorry I moved away.”

Nothing.

I pressed the receiver closer. “I don’t know how to keep you with me.”

Then came a soft click. Not from the phone, exactly. From somewhere in the box, or somewhere in me.

I thought of Grandma at the kitchen table, peeling an orange in one long strip. I thought of the way she said my name when she was pleased with me, as if it were a song with a familiar ending. I thought of the things she had taught me without calling them lessons: how to make soup from almost nothing, how to tell when a person wanted company, how to leave the last piece of cake for someone else and pretend not to notice.

I put down the receiver.

When I returned to the house, I asked my mother if I could call Grandma. She said yes, and I did. We talked about the weather and school. Then Grandma asked what I’d been thinking about.

“Nothing much,” I said.

“That’s something,” she replied.

Years passed. The apple tree eventually produced apples, though only three, and one was eaten by a bird before I could pick it. I grew taller. I made new friends. The old street became a place I visited, then a place I remembered, then a place I could find only in dreams.

I kept the stone shaped like a sleeping fox. I kept the cracked blue mug until the handle broke off. I still think of the red telephone box from time to time, standing at the end of the street with rain gathered on its roof.

I never learned whether it had answered me.

But I know this: when I have something I can’t say, I say it anyway. I say it in the kitchen while the kettle boils, or in the car when the road is dark, or to the quiet side of the bed before I fall asleep. I say it to people who are still here.

And sometimes, when the world is very still, I hear a small click, like a line connecting.
